--- title: "September 27–30, 2026" date: 2026-09-27 description: "Network median 1.85 in (range 1.30–3.19 in); peak IVT 388 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ from the SW; Polo within 1,500 km" categories: [IVT ≥ 250, Tropical cyclone nearby, Snow, Final] execute: freeze: auto --- ## Summary Most of the rain fell between overnight Monday, September 28, and overnight Wednesday, September 30, over about 48 hours. Rain gauges across Flagstaff caught a typical 1.85 inches, from 1.46 in at Rio de Flag @ Snowbowl Road to 3.19 in at Waterline Rd #1 (Lenox-Wupatki Trails). The airport measured 2.68 in, about 16 times the normal for those 4 days. Only 9 Septembers since 1898 had a wetter 4 days. Snow fell only at the highest mountain sites; in town it was rain. Nights were mild for the season, about 7 °F above normal. Moist air flowed from the southwest, drawn north by an area of low pressure aloft centred about 560 miles to the west-northwest. For part of the storm it was strong enough to count as an atmospheric river (a long, narrow stream of moist air), but most of the rain, 72%, fell outside those hours. 16 of 18 USGS gauges within 68 miles had daily flows above the 90th percentile for the date. The Little Colorado River near Winslow (6,910 cubic feet per second, or cfs) and Jacks Canyon Creek near Winslow (481 cfs) both peaked at about their typical yearly peaks (the median of annual peaks); Granite Creek at Prescott peaked at 1,180 cfs, about 70% of its typical yearly peak. (River flows are provisional.) ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Technical summary Across 37 gauges the event total ranged from 1.46 to 3.19 in (median 1.85 in). The central 80% of the network-mean rain fell between Sep 28 03:00 MST and Sep 30 03:00 MST (48 h). Moisture transport over Flagstaff reached atmospheric-river strength: ERA5 IVT was at or above 250 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ for 30 h and peaked at 388 kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹ from the SW at Sep 28 05:00 MST. 28% of the network-mean rain fell while IVT was at or above 250. Polo came within 649 km of Flagstaff (Sep 29 17:00 MST, remnant disturbance). At the IVT peak, 500-hPa flow over Flagstaff was from the SW at 29 m s⁻¹, and the 500-hPa trough axis along 35.25°N was at 120.8°W, 827 km west of Flagstaff (5,701 m, against 5,813 m over Flagstaff). A closed 500-hPa low (5,660 m) was centred 903 km to the WNW, at 37.8°N 121.2°W. The strongest 250-hPa wind within 1,000 km was 57 m s⁻¹, 650 km to the N. The 250-hPa wind over Flagstaff peaked at 45 m s⁻¹ (Sep 27 23:00 MST), 6 h before the IVT peak. ::: ## Rain across the network ::: {#38c20cca .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Event rain total at each city and county gauge (circle color and label show the total in inches; map cropped to the network) over shaded relief (USGS 3DEP), 200-m elevation contours, streams (USGS NHD) and highways (Census TIGER). Tap or click the map to open the frame full size.* ## What the forecasters said The National Weather Service office in Flagstaff discussed the moisture source in its Area Forecast Discussions as the event unfolded. Excerpts, quoted verbatim (links to the Iowa Environmental Mesonet archive): - **Sep 24, 10:16 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609250516)): "Moisture associated with two tropical cyclones (Hurricane Polo forecast to be off the southern Baja at this time and TS Odalys much farther west) will be pulled northeastward into the southwest United States in advance of this trough." - **Sep 26, 1:23 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609262023)): "Despite the fact the tropical moisture is coming from two tropical cyclones to the south, neither one of these circulations will actually make it up into Arizona." - **Sep 28, 11:43 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609281843)): "Current satellite imagery show a plume of moisture originating from the remnants of Odalys moving across northern Arizona. Meanwhile, Hurricane Polo is centered of the west coast of Southern Baja California." - **Sep 29, 2:03 PM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609292103)): "Arizona remains under a very dynamic weather pattern today with upper level low pressure centered over western Arizona and moisture from Hurricane Polo streaming northward." - **Sep 30, 2:12 AM MST** ([AFD](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/wx/afos/p.php?pil=AFDFGZ&e=202609300912)): "Water vapor satellite imagery show the upper-level low pressure centered over central Arizona and moving eastward, with moisture from the remnants of Polo now mostly being lifted into eastern New Mexico and western Texas." ## Climate context - **Airport precipitation:** 2.68 in over 4 local days, against a 1991–2020 normal of 0.17 in for those days (16× normal). - **Rank:** the 10th largest 4-day airport total in September among 129 years with data since 1898 (each year's largest 4-day total ending in September). - **Airport temperature:** highs averaged -9.2 °F and lows +7.0 °F relative to normal. - **Water year to date** (Oct 1, 2025 – Sep 30, 2026): airport 22.4 in (109% of normal);
